extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Reformation history and literary/biographical scholarship (general educated readers and historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical norms for composing or judging didactic/religious Colloquies and New Testament paraphrases (style, audience, doctrinal tact, and dissemination). Covers how to instruct while amusing, moral suitability for youth, use of satire, and accessibility of scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquies: instruct by amusing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Colloquies were written 'to instruct by amusing' and should combine humour with moral/didactic purpose; they 'touch upon every class of society and upon every vice and weakness of human nature' so that even comic or familiar passages carry a moral lesson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variety of tones (sparkling humour to plain didacticism); aim to instruct through dialogue and satire; beware later additions becoming 'downright dull' if overly didactic. Examples: Abbot and the Learned Lady (advocating women's education), Youth and the Harlot (realism used to reform the erring woman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and social breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Colloquies and paraphrases should address 'every class of society'—from clergy to laypeople—and adapt content and tone accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes/voices relatable to different social groups; choose topics (monks, schoolmen, superstitions, domestic life) apt to instruct a wide readership. Framing (dedications, prefaces) should signal intended audience and purpose (e.g., dedication to a young reader to show pedagogic intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral suitability for youth (censors' criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical/university censors evaluate works for danger to the morals of the young and for doctrinal conformity (e.g., the Sorbonne condemned the Colloquies as 'dangerous to the morals of the young' and akin to heretical writings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate institutional scrutiny: avoid language or examples likely to be judged 'godless' or corrupting; be aware that satire and frank realism may be taken as 'poison' aimed at youth (Luther's critique). Consequence: bans or forbidding students to read the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire and realism balanced with prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and realistic treatment of vice can be effective for moral reform but risk being read as attack on the Church or as corrupting youth; critics (e.g., Luther, Sorbonne) may interpret sharp humour as 'poison' or an assault on faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using satire, take into account how rhetorical irony might be received by different audiences; consider explicit framing or disclaimers if aiming to avoid accusations of heresy or immorality. Examples in text show satire directed at monks and superstitions but also producing official condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture accessibility: paraphrase and translation as valid strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring Scripture to the laity there are two legitimate approaches: (1) educate people in the original 'three tongues' (Hebrew, Greek, Latin) or (2) provide paraphrases/translations into the vernacular so common people can know Scripture in their own tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer accessibility for daily life (examples: farmer singing Psalms, weaver reading Gospels aloud). Paraphrases should be intelligible and edifying for lay readers and may be translated into common tongues for wide influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing doctrinal controversy: distinguish essentials from non-essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: When engaging controversial theological subjects (e.g., Eucharist), authors should draw a clear line between what is essential to the faith (creedal truths) and what is non-essential or historically developed expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State clearly which doctrines are core and which are formulations open to historical development or debate; this tactic can reduce charges of heterodoxy and place speculative issues in a context suitable for learned discussion rather than mass agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to Church consensus as a prudential standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus repeatedly asserts a readiness to 'conform to the requirements of the Roman Church' and to accept the 'consent of all Christian people' as a determining standard—i.e., public doctrinal conformity is a criterion for acceptable published positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contested matters, indicate willingness to accept authoritative Church judgment; frame private speculative remarks for learned friends and avoid presenting exploratory opinions as public dogma. Beware private conversations being publicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eucharist: subjects proper to learned debate vs laity faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex metaphysical questions about the Eucharist (listed as proper for 'those of trained intelligence') include: how the change of substance takes place; how accidents can exist without a substance; how bread/wine retain sensible qualities; when they begin/cease to be body and blood; whether another substance succeeds if the form is destroyed; how the same body may be in innumerable places; how a human body can be present under a crumb, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lay readers, it is enough to hold devotional belief in the real presence after consecration; reserve technical metaphysical discussion for learned treatises. Authors should signal the intended readership for such technical discussion to avoid popular confusion or censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly discretion: separate intimate discourse from public assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus defends free, candid inquiry among learned friends but insists that private speculations should not be presented as his public teaching; however, when such private remarks are reported publicly, they may be taken as author's dogma and provoke controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain prudence about which remarks are made in private forums versus printed works; avoid careless attributions, and be aware that ambiguous private statements can be weaponized by opponents (example: Pelicanus and rumours about Erasmus' views).
